title: UX review: demo report (Parcelly)
persona: Owner of a small online shop shipping 50–300 parcels a month; first visit, often on a phone between orders.

text.label: Demo report: “Parcelly” is a fictional shipping-label app; all pages, numbers and findings are made up
text.headline: Shop owners give up at the [[label price]]: it appears only after sign-up
text.lead: Three of five tasks finished, but the one that decides a purchase — what a label costs — fails on the public site, and connecting a store hides its error behind a spinner. Fix the price answer first, then the connection error and the phone checkout.
text.tasksNote: Each square is one step of a task, coloured by friction. Sign-up was stopped before the final button on purpose, so that step is marked “not tested”.
text.lensesH: Decision support and error states are the weakest lenses
text.lensesP: Scores 0–100 show how well the product already does on each UX lens; below 40 means people struggle. For a first-time shop owner, decision support, forms and mobile weigh most.
text.walkH: Five tasks, step by step, with three questions each
text.walkP: At every step: does the person know what to do, do they see that it worked, and can they recover from a wrong turn? Friction: 0 none, 1 minor, 2 major, 3 blocker.
text.heurH: Visibility of status and error recovery break most
text.heurP: How many issues break each of Nielsen's 10 heuristics, and the worst severity among them.
text.matrixH: {qw} quick wins with high impact and low effort
text.matrixP: Each dot is an issue from the table below. Filled dots are fixes; outlined red dots are rethinks that need a prototype and a test first.
text.opsP: Severity says how bad an issue is for the person (1 cosmetic to 4 blocker). ICE = impact × confidence × ease decides what to do first. The top three are highlighted.
text.nextH: Three fixes for the next sprint
text.nextP: Each has a hypothesis, a success metric and the cheapest way to check it.
text.planH: Full plan: all {n} issues, best value first
text.planP: For each issue: what we saw, the proposed change, steps, metric, effort, risk and a usability task that confirms the fix. The top three also have alternatives, a success threshold and a pre-mortem.
text.testH: Run these 5 tasks with 5 shop owners
text.testP: The walkthrough is one reviewer's judgment. This plan checks it with people who match the persona, before and after the fixes.
text.dataH: Confidence is medium: real-user data is a sample
text.dataP: Findings come from walking the product, a keyboard pass and a sample of analytics and support tickets. No session recordings and no tests with real users yet.
how: The owner named the persona and five tasks; one start question was skipped (see the answers).
Each task was walked in a browser at 1280px and repeated on a 390px phone view; nothing was submitted or paid.
Forms and error messages were read from the page; the store connection was tried with a test store.
The header and checkout were walked with the keyboard; an accessibility scanner ran on four pages.
Issues were tagged with Nielsen's heuristics, given a severity and ranked by ICE; the top three got alternatives, a threshold and a pre-mortem.

kpis.l: Of trial sign-ups start on a phone

tasks.goal: Say in one sentence what the app does and whether it fits a small shop.

steps.note: “Print cheaper shipping labels from your shop, in two clicks” names the job and the audience.
The video autoplays without captions; on a phone it starts muted with no hint that it has sound.
Logos of four platforms with a “See all integrations” link.

tasks.goal: Know what 200 labels a month would cost, all in.

steps.note: Plans show the monthly fee only; label prices say “See your rates after sign-up”.
No calculator and no example; the total cannot be worked out before creating an account.

steps.s: Look for the answer in help
steps.note: The help search for “label price” returns 0 results; the article is titled “Carrier rates explained”.

tasks.goal: Create an account and know what happens next.

steps.note: 9 fields, 6 required, including company VAT number and “How did you hear about us?”. Password rules appear only after an error.

steps.s: Check whether a card is needed
steps.note: “No card needed” is in the FAQ, not next to the form.
Not pressed by rule; the confirmation email was not tested.

tasks.goal: Connect a store and see my orders in Parcelly.

steps.note: The pop-up asks for 11 permissions with no note on why each is needed.
With a store that had no paid orders, the spinner ran for over 2 minutes and never said “No orders yet”.
“Reconnect” sits under Settings › Advanced; the error log says “Sync job 4 failed (code 0)”.

tasks.t: Buy and print the first label
tasks.goal: Buy a label for one order and print it.

steps.s: Open an order and pick a carrier
steps.note: Carriers sorted by name, not by price or delivery time.
Weight in grams and size in centimetres with no saved presets; on a phone the number fields open a full keyboard.
At 390px the “Buy label” button sits under a sticky chat bubble; tapping it opens the chat.
PDF opens with a clear “Print” button and a 4×6 option.

ops.t: Show label prices and a monthly cost calculator on the pricing page
Replace the endless import spinner with a clear empty state
Move the chat bubble off the “Buy label” button on phones
Cut sign-up to 3 fields and show password rules up front
Write a plain error and a visible “Reconnect” button for failed syncs
Say “No card needed” next to the sign-up button
Sort carriers by price and add parcel presets
Use number keypads and units in the parcel fields on phones
Make help search understand shop owners' words
Explain each store permission in one line
Add captions and a sound hint to the demo video
A rates preview without an account: paste a postcode, see real label prices

1.h: If shop owners can see label prices and a monthly total before signing up, more of them will start a trial, because the price is the question that decides whether to try.
1.m: Pricing page → trial start rate; share of test participants who can state a monthly total
1.t: Add a static rates table and a 3-input calculator; compare 2 weeks of trial starts from /pricing with the 2 weeks before

2.h: If an empty store shows “No paid orders yet — create a test order” within 10 seconds, new users will not abandon the connection step, because they will know it worked.
2.m: Share of new accounts that reach the first order screen in the first session
2.t: Ship the empty state behind a flag for half of new accounts for 2 weeks

3.h: If the chat bubble moves above the bottom bar during checkout, phone users will reach “Buy label” on the first tap, because nothing covers it.
3.m: Mis-taps that open chat on /app/checkout; label purchases from phones
3.t: One-line CSS change; compare chat opens from checkout a week before and after

1.why: /pricing lists three monthly plans; label prices say “See your rates after sign-up”. There is no calculator or example. Support sample: 23 of 120 pre-sale tickets ask what a label costs.
1.change: A rates block under the plans: typical label prices per carrier for common parcel sizes, and a calculator (labels per month, average weight, destination) that shows the monthly total including the plan fee.
steps: Agree with carriers which rates may be shown publicly; show ranges where exact rates differ by account.
Add a rates table for 3 parcel sizes and the 4 main carriers.
Add a calculator with 3 inputs that returns plan + labels = monthly total.
Link “What will 200 labels cost?” from the home page and the help article.
1.metric: Trial starts per 100 pricing-page visits; pre-sale tickets about label price
1.risk: Shown rates must stay current: pull them from the same source as the app, never type them in.

test.task: “You ship about 200 small parcels a month. How much would Parcelly cost you?” Start on the home page.
test.success: States a monthly total within 2 minutes without creating an account.
test.watch: Whether they trust the number; which inputs confuse them.

alt: A “from $0.xx per label” line only — rejected: still no total for the owner's volume.
A rates PDF — rejected: does not answer “what will I pay” and goes stale.
1.thr: Trial starts from /pricing up by at least 15%, and 4 of 5 test participants state a total within 2 minutes
1.pm: It failed because the shown rates differed from the rates after sign-up and users felt misled. So pull the table from the live rate service and label it “typical rates, yours may be lower”.
copy: “What will 200 labels cost? Work it out in 10 seconds”: uses the persona's own question.
“Plan + labels = your monthly total”: explains the two parts of the price in one line.
accept: /pricing shows label prices without an account
The calculator total equals plan fee + labels × rate from the live rate service

2.why: After connecting a store with no paid orders, /app/orders showed a spinner for over 2 minutes and never changed. Nothing said the connection worked or that the store simply had no orders.
2.change: Within 10 seconds of connecting: either the imported orders, or an empty state saying “Connected. No paid orders yet” with a button to create a test order and a link to help.
steps: Return an explicit “zero orders” result from the import instead of waiting.
Show the empty state with a test-order button.
Time out after 30 seconds with a plain error and “Try again”.
Log empty, error and timeout cases separately.
2.metric: Share of new accounts that reach the first order screen in the first session
2.risk: Showing “No orders” while a slow import is still running; wait for the import's own result.

test.task: Connect this test store (it has no paid orders) and tell me when you are ready to ship.
test.success: Understands within 15 seconds that the store is connected and empty.
test.watch: Refreshing the page; going back to connect again.

alt: A progress bar — rejected: there is nothing to show progress on for an empty store.
An email when the import finishes — kept as a later addition for large stores.
2.thr: Abandonment at the import step down by half, and 5 of 5 participants understand the empty state
2.pm: It failed because large stores import slowly and now see a false timeout. So set the timeout by order count and show progress for big imports.
accept: An empty store shows the empty state within 10 seconds
A failed import shows a plain error and “Try again” within 30 seconds

3.why: At 390px the sticky chat bubble covers the right half of the “Buy label” button on /app/checkout; tapping it opened the chat. Analytics sample: 41% of trial sign-ups start on a phone.
3.change: On checkout screens the chat bubble moves above the bottom action bar, or collapses into a “Help” link in the header.
steps: Hide or move the bubble on /app/checkout at widths under 600px.
Make the “Buy label” button full width with 48px height.
Check with a 360px and a 390px screen.
3.metric: Chat opens from /app/checkout on phones; phone label purchases
3.risk: Less visible help during payment; keep “Help” in the header.

test.task: On a phone: buy the label for order #1.
test.success: Taps “Buy label” on the first try.

alt: Shrink the bubble — rejected: still covers part of the button.
Remove chat in the app — rejected: users need help during their first label.
3.thr: Chat opens from checkout on phones down by 80% with no drop in help requests elsewhere
3.pm: It failed because the chat vendor's script re-positioned the bubble after load. So set the position through the vendor's settings, not only in CSS.
accept: The button is at least 48px tall

4.why: /signup has 9 fields, 6 required, including a company VAT number and “How did you hear about us?”. Password rules (12 characters, one number) appear only after a failed attempt.
4.change: Email, password and shop platform only; the rest asked later inside the app when needed. Password rules shown under the field before typing.
steps: Remove VAT number, company size and source from sign-up; ask for VAT at first invoice.
Show the password rules under the field and tick them off as they are met.
Add autocomplete attributes (email, new-password).
4.metric: Sign-up form completion rate; errors per sign-up
4.risk: Marketing loses the “how did you hear” answer; ask it after the first label instead.

test.task: Create an account for your shop; stop before the last button.
test.success: Fills the form in under a minute without an error.
test.watch: Pauses at optional fields; reaction to password rules.

5.why: When sync fails, the only message is “Sync job 4 failed (code 0)” in Settings › Advanced, where “Reconnect” also lives. The orders screen shows nothing.
5.change: A banner on the orders screen: what failed in plain words, and a “Reconnect” button right there.
steps: Map sync error codes to 4 plain messages (permission removed, store offline, timeout, unknown).
Show a banner on /app/orders with the message and “Reconnect”.
Keep the technical code in a “Details” toggle for support.
5.metric: Time from a sync failure to the next successful sync
5.risk: Too many banners for short outages; show after 2 failed attempts.

test.task: Your orders stopped appearing. Get them back.
test.success: Reconnects from the banner within 1 minute.
test.watch: Whether they go to Settings first.

6.why: The sign-up page does not say whether a card is needed; the answer “No card needed” is in the pricing FAQ.
6.change: “No card needed — 14 days free” as a line under the “Create account” button.
steps: Add the line under the button on /signup and on the home-page CTA.
Remove the duplicate FAQ answer or link to it.
6.risk: Only if it is true for every plan.

test.task: Before signing up: “Will this charge you anything today?”
test.success: Answers correctly without leaving the page.

7.why: Carriers are listed by name. Parcel size has to be typed every time; there are no presets.
7.change: Carriers sorted by price with delivery time shown; up to 5 saved parcel presets.
steps: Sort by price by default with a toggle for speed.
Add “Save as preset” to the parcel form.
Pre-fill the last used preset.
7.risk: Cheapest is not always best; show delivery days next to price.

test.task: Ship order #2, same box as last time, cheapest option.

8.why: At 390px the weight and size fields open a full text keyboard and show no units next to the numbers.
8.change: Numeric keypads (inputmode="decimal") and units shown inside the fields.
steps: Set inputmode="decimal" on weight and size.
Show “g” and “cm” as suffixes.
Check on iOS and Android.
8.metric: Errors in parcel size per label

test.task: On a phone: enter a 1.2 kg, 30×20×10 cm parcel.
test.success: Enters it in one go without switching keyboards.

9.why: Help search for “label price” returns 0 results; the article that answers it is titled “Carrier rates explained”.
9.change: Help search that maps shop owners' words to the right articles, and article titles in their words.
steps: Add synonyms: label price → carrier rates, cost, fee.
Rename the article “What a label costs”.
Review zero-result searches monthly.

test.task: Find in help what a label to Germany costs.
test.success: Opens the right article from the first search.

10.why: The platform pop-up lists 11 permissions; Parcelly does not explain why it needs them. Whether this stops people is a hypothesis: no data on drop-off at this step.
10.change: Before the pop-up, a short list of what Parcelly reads and writes and why.
steps: Write one line per permission group.
Show it on /app/connect before redirecting.
Track how many cancel in the pop-up.
10.metric: Share who cancel at the platform pop-up
10.risk: A long list can scare more than it reassures; keep it to 4 lines.

test.task: Connect your shop. Would you approve this? Why?
test.success: Approves and can say why access is needed.

11.why: The home-page video autoplays without captions; on a phone it starts muted with no sign that it has sound. The scanner flagged the video as having no captions track.
11.change: Captions on by default and a visible “Sound on” control.
steps: Add a captions track.
Show a “Sound on” button on muted playback.

test.task: Watch the video on a phone in a quiet room. What did it say?

12.why: Even with a rates table (#1) owners want their own numbers. A preview that takes a postcode and parcel size and shows live rates without an account might convince more; untested.
12.change: A public “Check your rates” page: from and to postcodes, parcel size, then live label prices and the monthly total.
steps: Prototype with live rates for one carrier.
Test with 5 owners against the rates table.
Build only if it beats #1 on confidence and trial starts.
12.metric: Trial starts after a rates check
12.risk: API cost and abuse of a public rates endpoint; rate-limit it.

test.task: Find out exactly what your usual parcel would cost to ship.
test.success: Gets a price they trust and wants to start a trial.
test.watch: Whether they mind entering a postcode.

testplan.who: Owners or managers of small online shops shipping 50–300 parcels a month, not Parcelly users; 3 on a phone, 2 on a laptop.
testplan.n: 5 sessions of 40 minutes; repeat with 5 new people after the top fixes
testplan.method: Moderated remote, think-aloud, screen sharing; a test store for task 4. Read each task aloud; do not help.
testplan.before: Consent to record; explain we test the app, not them; ask how they ship today.

tasks.t: A friend recommended Parcelly. Take a minute and tell me what it does and whether it fits your shop.
tasks.success: Describes label printing for small shops in their own words.
tasks.watch: Whether they play the video; what they skip.
ask: Who do you think this is for?

tasks.t: You ship about 200 small parcels a month. Find out what Parcelly would cost you.
tasks.success: States a monthly total without creating an account.
tasks.watch: Where they look for label prices; reaction to “after sign-up”.
ask: How sure are you of that number (1–7)?
What would stop you from trying it?

tasks.t: You want to try it. Get to the point where you would create the account, then stop.
tasks.success: Completes the form in under a minute and knows whether a card is needed.
ask: What do you expect to happen next?

tasks.t: Connect this test store and get ready to ship your first order.
tasks.success: Understands the store is connected and has no paid orders.
ask: At which moment did you know it worked?

tasks.t: Ship order #1 with the cheapest option and print the label.
tasks.start: Orders screen with one test order
tasks.success: Prints a label in under 2 minutes.
tasks.watch: Carrier choice; parcel fields; the chat bubble on phones.
ask: What would make this faster next time?

measure: Task success: done, done with help, not done
Single Ease Question (SEQ, 1–7) after each task
Wrong turns and taps that open chat
testplan.after: Match each failure to a walkthrough step; raise or lower confidence on the matching issues; re-run tasks 2, 4 and 5 after the top three fixes.

answers.a: Small shop owners, 50–300 parcels a month, often on a phone
Understand, price, trial, connect store, first label
Skipped. Assumption: no usability tests yet

rules: Do not buy real labels or connect real customer stores while testing; use the test store and test payment mode.
Rates shown publicly must come from the live rate service, never typed by hand.
Record before/after screenshots at 1280px and 390px and a keyboard pass for every changed control.
Stay within UX: visual polish goes to a UI review, pricing strategy to a product review.
For a hypothesis or rethink task, prototype and test first; stop if the threshold is not met.

ICE.d: Impact × Confidence × Ease, each 1–10. The higher the product, the sooner to do it.

Nielsen's 10 heuristics.d: Ten general principles for interface design by Jakob Nielsen, such as visibility of system status and error prevention. Each issue here is tagged H1–H10.

heuristics.d: Here, Nielsen's 10 principles; H1–H10 in the tables.

Severity.d: 1 cosmetic, 2 minor (slows down), 3 major (many struggle or give up), 4 blocker (cannot be done this way).

empty state.d: What a screen shows when there is no data, such as a store with no orders. A good one says why and what to do next.

inputmode.d: An HTML attribute that tells a phone which keyboard to show, such as numbers only.

autocomplete.d: An attribute that tells the browser what a field is so it can fill it in.

think-aloud.d: Participants speak their thoughts while doing a task, so you hear why they hesitate.

SEQ.d: Single Ease Question: “Overall, how easy was this task?” on a 1–7 scale.

pre-mortem.d: Assume the fix failed three months from now and explain why; the reasons become checks to do first.

FAQ.d: Frequently asked questions; here, on the pricing page.

IA.d: How content is grouped, named and linked, so people can predict where things are.

VAT.d: A company tax number; here asked at sign-up although it is only needed for invoices.
